title: Food and hosting
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

allowedPatterns: Je voudrais + du/de la/des + N + , + s'il vous plaît
Je ne veux pas de + N

rules.text: AFTER A NEGATION EVERY PARTITIVE COLLAPSES TO de. Je ne veux pas DE café, Il n'y a pas DE pain, Je ne mange pas DE viande. L1-M3 taught du, de la and des, and L1-M3 taught ne … pas, and the two never met in one sentence until now. This is one of the few French rules with no exception worth a learner's time, and Je ne veux pas du café is what every English speaker writes who has not been told.

FRENCH HAS A SECOND SET OF PRONOUNS for standing alone and for following a preposition: moi, toi. Pour moi, un café — je and tu cannot go there at all. They are also what you use to answer a question with one word: Qui veut du café? — Moi.

The object pronouns open narrowly, and the index decides how: me and te are free words, but le, la and les are already L1-M1's ARTICLES, so the identically spelled object pronouns can never be first-taught here. The placement law is shown on me and te — Vous pouvez me donner…? — and the rest of the series is L3's.

Ordering is M1's frozen je voudrais plus L1's partitives, and the register point is the same one M1 made: Je veux un café is grammatical and lands as a demand. Je voudrais and Pour moi are what people actually say at a counter.

A FRENCH REFUSAL IS SOFTENED BY A COMPLIMENT, not by a reason. Non merci, c'était très bon · C'est très gentil, mais ça va. A host offers once or twice and then stops — which is a genuinely different shape from the Indian and Russian hosting the other courses in this collection describe, where the offer is expected to be repeated.

sentences.display: Je voudrais du pain, s'il vous plaît

words.note: Not a sum. L'addition, s'il vous plaît is how a meal ends, and the elided form is its own index key.

sentences.trap: du is not "some" as a separate word — it is de plus le, welded, and it means an unspecified amount of something. L1-M3 taught it and this module is where it meets a negation.
sentences.sound: zhuh voo-DRAY dü PAN. The ü is rounded and the an of pain is nasal.

sentences.display: Je ne veux pas de café
sentences.literal: I not want not of coffee

words.note: L1-M1's de doing a second job. After ne … pas every partitive collapses to this — du, de la and des all become de, with no exception worth learning.
Feminine, so de la viande — until a negation flattens it to de viande.

sentences.trap: Je ne veux pas du café is what an English speaker writes and it is wrong. The negation eats the article, and nothing survives of it but the de.
sentences.sound: zhuh nuh vuh pa duh ka-FAY. The whole line runs flat until the last syllable.

sentences.usage: Turning something down, or saying what you do not eat.

words.note: A preposition, and it is what forces the stressed pronoun: pour moi, never pour je. It also does purpose — pour manger, in order to eat.
The stressed pronoun. je cannot follow a preposition or stand alone, so pour moi and Moi? both need this word instead.
moi's tu partner. Et toi? is how a question gets turned back, and it is one of the commonest two words in French.

sentences.trap: pour je is not French at all. A preposition needs the stressed form, and that is a whole second set of pronouns rather than a variant of the first.
sentences.sound: poor MWA un ka-FAY. moi is one syllable and takes the weight of the phrase.

sentences.display: Vous pouvez me donner du pain?
sentences.cue: Could you give me some bread?
sentences.literal: You can me to-give of-the bread?

words.note: The object pronoun, and it goes IN FRONT of the verb it belongs to — here the infinitive donner. Before a vowel it elides to m'.
A regular -er infinitive. It takes a thing and a person: donner du pain à quelqu'un, or with a pronoun in front, me donner du pain.

sentences.trap: me sits between pouvez and donner, where English would put nothing. French object pronouns go in front of the verb they belong to, and here that verb is the infinitive.
sentences.sound: voo poo-VAY muh do-NAY dü PAN. me is short and leans onto the verb.

words.note: Three jobs on one word. Encore du café? is the offer; il est encore là is "he's still there", and the sentence says which.
What a waiter says: Vous désirez? It is more formal than vouloir and is almost only heard in that one question.

sentences.trap: The offer is made with encore rather than with a word for "more", which keeps plus free for the comparative M9 needs. Encore is what a host actually says.
sentences.sound: on-KOR dü ka-FAY. The en is nasal and the r is at the back.

sentences.display: Je voudrais du poisson, pas de viande
sentences.literal: I would-like of-the fish, not of meat

words.note: With one s it would be poison, which means what it looks like. The double s is what keeps them apart, and it is heard.
Masculine and plural in ordinary use: des légumes. The singular is heard mostly in a shop's labelling.

sentences.trap: One sentence, both halves of the rule: du poisson where there is no negation, de viande where there is. Nothing else in the sentence changed.
sentences.sound: dü pwa-SON pa duh VYAND. The double s is a hiss and the single s of poison would be a z.

sentences.display: Un verre d'eau, s'il vous plaît

words.note: Feminine, and it starts with a vowel — l'assiette. Une assiette de soupe is a plate of soup, with de and no article.

sentences.trap: d'eau is L1-M8's own key, one token with the apostrophe inside it. A container plus de plus a bare noun is the shape, and the article never comes back.
sentences.sound: un VEHR DO seel voo PLEH. d'eau is one syllable with a pure o.

sentences.cue: Could you give me the bill?

words.note: me's tu partner, and it goes in the same place — in front of the verb. Before a vowel it elides to t'.
Two s's, and both are heard as a hiss. With one it would be désert, a desert — the same trap as poisson and poison.

sentences.trap: The bill has to be asked for. A French waiter will not bring it unprompted, and this is the sentence that ends every meal.
sentences.sound: voo poo-VAY muh do-NAY la-dee-SYON. The elision joins l' straight onto addition.

sentences.display: Il n'y a pas de dessert
sentences.literal: It not-there has not of dessert

words.cue: not there (in il n'y a pas)
words.note: L1-M7's il y a with ne squeezed into it and elided: il n'y a pas. The apostrophe fuses ne and y into one token, so this is its own index key.
The z is silent, so it sounds like ri. Its plural is also riz — a word ending in z never adds an s.

sentences.trap: L1-M7's il y a is negated here, and the partitive goes flat with it. Three separate L1 pieces meet in this one sentence and none of them is new.
sentences.sound: eel nya pa duh de-SEHR. The n'y a runs together as a single syllable.
